title: kv-cache-reuse-eviction-bw-analysis
content:
Summary:

Quick notes from profiling runs focused on KV cache behavior across conversational/instruction workloads. Goal: identify primary causes of low reuse and memory bandwidth bottlenecks, validate eviction/paging impacts, and propose short-term mitigations + benchmark plan. This is a working doc (notes + raw numbers).

Key observations (high level):
- Reuse rates vary widely by workload: 18–48% effective KV hit depending on prefix distributions. Chat-style workloads with long context and repeated prefixes hit higher (30–48%); instruction/one-shot workloads are low (~18–25%).
- When KV working set exceeds per-shard GPU allocation we observe two distinct behaviors: (1) increased eviction churn causing repeated recomputation and higher latency variance, (2) CPU-GPU paging activity (cudaMemcpy stalls) that shows up as 30–200ms spikes per request in worst-case traces.
- Memory bandwidth appears to be a secondary limiting factor for large-batch prefilling / KV reconstruction after eviction. On our A100 test nodes the kernel-bound phases reach ~40–60% of measured device peak BW during KV rebuilds, and sustained memcpy phases saturate the host-device link leading to queuing.
- Current eviction policy (per-shard LRU with fixed per-shard cap) causes pathological thrash in multi-tenant shards where hot prefixes are unevenly distributed.

Environment / test setup:
- Models: 13B candidate model (quantized FP16 path + KV caching enabled) + a 30B variant for stress tests.
- Nodes: 1x A100-80GB (dev) and 2x A100-80GB in our staging cluster for multi-GPU sharding tests.
- Tools: Nsight Systems for timeline traces, ncu for kernel-level sampling, perf / bpftrace for CPU hotspots, custom runtime tracing for KV hits/evictions (trace ids attached).
- Synthetic workloads:
  - "chat-long": 75–150 token prefixes reused across sessions, high token overlap.
  - "chat-short-heavy": many short distinct prefixes (5–20 tokens) high QPS.
  - "instr-one-shot": one-turn instructions, low reuse.

Detailed findings / numbers (representative):
- chat-long (single-shard): reuse 45%, median 95th latency 120ms, evictions per-minute 12, KV rebuild windows account for ~18% of CPU time.
- chat-short-heavy (multi-tenant shard): reuse 21%, 95th latency 310ms, eviction churn high (eviction rate ~0.9 of insert rate), observed paging stalls up to 200ms on some requests.
- instr-one-shot: reuse 19%, 95th latency 140ms, rebuilds less frequent but per-rebuild cost similar to chat-long.
- Memory BW: during KV rebuilds kernels measured ~45% of reported device BW; memcpy host->device phases show bursty throughput and queueing, correlating with latency spikes.

Root cause hypotheses:
1) Per-shard fixed caps + global unevenness => hot prefixes evicted prematurely while cold prefixes occupy space. LRU favors recency, not frequency for these access patterns.
2) When eviction causes recompute of KV for long prefixes we do a full prefilling path that is both compute and memory heavy (dense key/value writes into GPU memory) causing bursts that compete with other kernels for BW.
3) Paging/prefetch path is synchronous in critical codepaths; cudaMemcpy and kernel launches block request handling, amplifying tail latency.

Short-term mitigations (can be implemented in next 1–3 sprints):
- Increase per-shard KV cap by 10–25% for heavy chat shards (configurable override) to reduce eviction churn for predictable tenants. Quick win for high reuse workloads.
- Implement LFU-ish eviction with time decay (cheap approximate counters) for multi-tenant shards to prioritize frequently-reused prefixes over recently-seen cold prefixes.
- Make KV prefill asynchronous: start prefill on a background stream and return early with partial KV while continuing to fill rest; add graceful fallback policy to allow generation to proceed with partial KV. (Risk: correctness + slight quality variance; needs test harness.)
- Introduce an adaptive rebuild throttle that limits concurrent KV rebuilds per GPU to bound memory BW pressure; queue excess rebuilds with prioritization.

Medium-term changes (3–6 months):
- On-device KV compression: store keys/values in a compressed format (quantized or delta-encoded) to reduce footprint and memcpy volume. Evaluate CPU/GPU decompression overhead vs memory BW savings.
- Offload cold KV to host-pinned memory with async GPUDirect and prefetch heuristics to reduce on-device footprint while avoiding full synchronous paging.
- Smarter sharding (hot-key collocation): route requests so hot prefixes land on the same shard subset minimizing cross-shard duplication and eviction. Needs integration with routing layer.

Benchmark plan (microbench harness):
- Build a KV trace replay harness (JMH-like for inference) that can replay synthetic and sampled real traces (from prod sampling: RT-4382) with configurable reuse distributions, prefix lengths, and concurrency.
- Microbench suites:
  - Reuse sweep: vary reuse % (10–80%) and measure per-request latency, KV hit/miss, and eviction churn.
  - Eviction policy comparison: LRU vs LFU-decay vs weighted LRU under multi-tenant load.
  - Paging stress: artificially inflate working set to trigger host-GPU paging and measure tail latency and BW usage.
  - Rebuild concurrency sweep: control parallel rebuilds and measure effect on other requests and BW.

Open questions / risks:
- Quality impact of partial KV (prefill async) needs a controlled evaluation: does partial context materially change token probabilities in representative tasks? We need to run the same evals used by Optimize.
- LFU counters add memory overhead; need to benchmark overhead vs hit improvement. Consider approximate counters (bloom-ish or count-min sketches).
- Interactions with quantization paths: compressed KVs may change numerical behavior; need regression tests.

Immediate action items:
- (Ravi) Add LFU-decay PoC to runtime (RT-4399), include microbench comparison against existing LRU for a 2-hour run on staging cluster.
- (Maya) Build trace replay harness and synthetic workload generator; capture a 24h sample of real prefixes (sanitized) for replay (RT-4382).
- (Daniel) Prototype async prefill path + partial-KV fallback on a dev node and run evals for quality regression.
- (Elena) Coordinate bandwidth-limited stress tests and gather Nsight traces; attach raw traces to RT-4401.

Notes / links:
- See attached PR for runtime tracing hooks: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/1275
- Confluence design notes: KV cache design + eviction rationale: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/SERVE/KV+Cache+Design+Notes
- Jira tickets: RT-4382 (trace capture), RT-4399 (eviction PoC), RT-4401 (bandwidth traces)

Raw trace highlights (copied snippets):
- Example timeline: 0–12ms token gen kernel, 12–36ms KV rebuild memcpy + kernels, 36–60ms final decode kernels. When rebuilds overlap across N requests, decode kernels queue and 95th jumps 3–4x.
- Eviction log sample: shard-17 evicted prefix X multiple times in 30s window; rebuilds correspond to two different tenant flows converging on same hot prefix.

Conclusion:
We have identified eviction churn and synchronous rebuild/paging as the dominant contributors to tail latency under high working-set conditions. Short-term mitigations (cap tuning, LFU-decay, async prefill, rebuild throttling) should reduce tail while longer-term work (compression, host-pinned prefetched store, smarter sharding) will address capacity and cost. Next: get PoCs running and use the trace replay harness to quantify gains.

- Validate LFU memory overhead on 80GB nodes (Ravi).

(End of doc)
